extracted.intended_audience: physicians, neurologists, and medical researchers interested in hysteria, trance states, and unusual neuroses
extracted.subtask_description: A late-19th-century clinical/observational investigation reporting experiments, phenomenology, differential diagnosis, heredity, prognosis, and methodological cautions about the so-called 'Jumpers' (Jumping Frenchmen) of Maine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six sources of error in experimenting with living human beings
rubrics_metrics.description: The six sources of error in experimenting with living human beings are — 1. Unconscious deception on the part of the subject experimented on; 2. Intentional deception on the part of the subject experimented on; 3. Intentional collusion of other parties; 4. Unintentional collusion of other parties; 5. Chances and coincidences; 6. Phenomena of the involuntary life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states these apply to all experiments with human beings and notes that, in experimenting with the Jumpers, the nature of the phenomena made it easy to eliminate intentional deception because, unless the subject is surprised, the phenomena do not appear. Use this list as a checklist to eliminate or control possible sources of experimental error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exclusion and repeatability to establish involuntary action
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions were established 'by exclusion' — proving that only the involuntary action of mind on body could produce the phenomena — and experiments were 'repeated again and again, under various conditions at different times' to satisfy the investigator that error elements were eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that (a) vary conditions and times, (b) reproduce the phenomena reliably, and (c) systematically exclude alternative explanations (deception, collusion, coincidence, involuntary life phenomena) before concluding the action is involuntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliciting triggers and role of warning/preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomena are typically produced by unexpected, sharp, sudden stimuli (a slap, a sudden sound, a command uttered quickly and loudly). If the subject is warned or prepared (forewarned), the response is greatly reduced or absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing susceptibility, differentiate between surprised/unexpected stimuli (which elicit full responses) and expected/visible stimuli (which elicit only slight movements). Any experimental protocol must control for forewarning to avoid false negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenological diagnostic features (explosive movements and cries)
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts are 'explosive' and 'instantaneous' — throwing, striking, dropping, crying, jerking, lifting shoulders occur in but a second or so; movements are like 'the explosion of a gun' and include a characteristic cry resembling that in hysteria or epilepsy. The face may show temporary flushing or pallor or no change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these specific qualitative features (speed, impulsiveness, associated cry, brief duration, combination of motor acts) to identify and describe the disorder; note that the movements are difficult to imitate artificially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential diagnosis vs trance, hysteria, and epileptoform disorders
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jumpers differ from mesmeric/trance and some hysteric phenomena in two main respects: (1) the momentary character of the manifestations (actions last a second or so and the subject quickly returns to prior state), and (2) the persistence/permanence of liability to be excited (habit remains lifelong — 'once a Jumper, always a Jumper'—whereas epidemics of jerking or trance-related phenomena are time-limited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these two distinguishing criteria when differentiating jumping from longer-lasting trance/hysteria or episodic epidemic chorea; consider duration of individual events and lifelong susceptibility in diagnostic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as a psychical (mental), functional nervous disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Jumping is 'a psychical or mental form of nervous disease, and is of a functional character.' The best analogue is psychical hysteria (the 'servant-girl hysteria'), as opposed to the neurasthenic/anaemic (physical) form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the disorder primarily on psychological/functional grounds rather than as a degenerative/structural nervous disease unless structural evidence emerges; consider psychological frameworks for study and management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary tendency as an evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Jumping is observed to be 'fully as hereditary as insanity, or epilepsy, or hay-fever' — multiple affected members in families traced back generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take detailed family histories and consider heredity as a significant factor in evaluating cases; familial clustering supports a heritable susceptibility model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prognosis: lifelong liability and variability of susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: After the habit is formed the subject 'is always capable of displaying the phenomena in a greater or less degree at any moment' — susceptibility varies with time (worse with teasing/exertion, better after rest) but the liability tends to persist indefinitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise that prognosis includes persistent susceptibility with fluctuating severity; management may aim to reduce exposure to triggers and provide rest to lessen frequency/intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical consequences and risk assessment (self-harm and danger to others)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jumpers may perform dangerous acts when jumped: near self-injury (almost cut throat while shaving), smashing glass with fists, jumping into fire or water, dropping hot plates on others. Repeated jumping causes exhaustion and worsens their condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess situational risks carefully (dangerous objects, open flames, heights) and consider protective measures and counseling to minimize teasing/annoyance; include fatigue/exhaustion as an adverse outcome metric.
